newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Branson not lodging formal complaint against SAS.
newsitem.headline: Branson not lodging formal complaint against SAS.

text.p: British entrepreneur Richard Branson said on Tuesday he was not aiming to lodge a formal complaint against Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS) which he said was flouting European competition rules.

Earlier on Tuesday, SAS rejected accusations by Branson's Virgin Express regional airline that SAS was unfairly cutting the cost of tickets between Brussels and Copenhagen, but only for flights coinciding with the cheap Virgin flights.
Branson said he was writing a letter to the European Commission "at this moment" pointing out the selective SAS fare cuts.

"(But) rather than going through a formal complaint situation I hope they would just drop a line to SAS," he told a news conference here to promote the launch of Virgin Express's Brussels-Copenhagen link.
"We hope it will be settled in a sensible way," he added.

"What (SAS) should accept is that in most businesses there are more than just two players...but four, five, six, seven competing. There is plenty of room for people to fly on SAS flights, to fly on Virgin flights," he said.
But Branson warned SAS not to "play dirty" by undercutting prices on the Brussels-Copenhagen route.
Brussels-based Virgin Express, launched in April after Branson bought 90 percent of EuroBelgian Airlines SA (EBA), currently operates 14 Boeing 737 planes.
Branson said he expected Virgin Express to more than double the number of its planes by the turn of the century.
Virgin Express takes delivery of two new Boeing 737-400s early next year but these will replace two existing planes.
Branson said it was not yet clear whether Virgin Express would stick to Boeing planes. "It could also be mixed," he said.
He said he would welcome the development of "Super Jumbo" jets and order them for his Virgin Atlantic Airways trans-atlantic airline.
"We've actually said to Boeing we would like to be one of their launch customers," Branson said.
Planemakers like Boeing, McDonnel Douglas and European aircraft consortium Airbus plan to introduce jumbo planes that will dwarf the Boeing B747 now in use.

"We would like it to happen. (Airport) slots become scarce and even without low-fare travel the forecast is that twice as many people will be travelling by air by 2003. If you add low fare travel on top of that there will be enormous demand."
The new generation of large aircraft would seat 600 people against 400 for the B747-400.
Branson added he was not ruling out a closer "relationship" with another airline.
"What we won't be doing is forming an alliance which gives us a monopolistic dominance. Having said that, we may well have relationships with other airlines in the future," he said.
Branson said Virgin Express had an 85-percent seat occupancy rate due to its fares which underprice normal ticket prices by up to 75 percent.
"If we charged the full fare on Virgin Express, only 33 percent of our seats would be full. As it is, we are selling 85 percent and we're making profits," he said.
